players.product: Power-secured HPC/AI data-center lease campuses (Lake Mariner NY for Fluidstack/Google; Justified & Muskie KY) - ex-Bitcoin-mining conversion

quarterly_data.signal: CFO Patrick Fleury: fourth-quarter 2025 revenue was $35.8 million, down from $50.6 million in Q3 on lower Bitcoin production, while HPC lease revenue rose to $9.7 million, up 35% from $7.2 million in Q3. Full-year revenue increased 20% to $168.5 million, with digital asset revenue of $151.6 million and HPC lease revenue of $16.9 million. HPC leasing commenced in July 2025 and 18 megawatts of critical IT capacity were energized as of year-end; revenue mix will keep shifting toward contracted HPC revenue as buildings come online.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 revenue $35.8 million (vs $50.6 million Q3); HPC lease revenue $9.7 million, up 35% from $7.2 million; FY2025 revenue $168.5 million (+20%), of which HPC lease $16.9 million; 18 megawatts critical IT energized at year-end

quarterly_data.signal: HPC leasing profitability and losses (CFO Fleury): the as-reported 2025 HPC leasing segment profit margin was approximately 42% versus long-term guidance of approximately 85%, driven by $1.2 million of tenant fit-out revenue, $4.1 million of development and pre-revenue operating costs and partial-period revenue as buildings ramp; adjusting for those gives approximately 77%. 2025 adjusted EBITDA was negative $23.1 million (vs positive $60.4 million in 2024) and the GAAP net loss was $661.4 million, mainly from a $429.8 million non-cash fair-value loss tied largely to the Google warrant plus depreciation.
quarterly_data.figure: HPC segment margin approximately 42% reported / approximately 77% adjusted vs approximately 85% target; adjusted EBITDA negative $23.1 million; GAAP net loss $661.4 million incl. $429.8 million warrant/derivative loss

quarterly_data.signal: Lake Mariner Core42 delivery (CTO Nazar Khan): WULF Den and CB1 were delivered in the third quarter and generated revenue throughout Q4; CB2A is operational and CB2B is expected to be fully online in March, so all Core42 capacity will be energized and revenue producing by the end of the first quarter. Core42 requested incremental fit-out enhancements after contract execution; sequencing was adjusted, the monthly recurring charge was revised and no penalties were triggered.

Financing and project funding (CFO Fleury): in the second half of 2025 TeraWulf secured over $12.8 billion of HPC lease agreements and executed $6.5 billion of debt and equity-linked financing. Cash and restricted cash were $3.7 billion at December 31, 2025; the HoldCo parent had approximately $500 million of available cash as of January 31, 2026 (approximately $300 million pro forma for the Kentucky acquisition). WULF Compute had approximately $3 billion of gross cash with $850 million of CapEx spend complete and $2.38 billion remaining (approximately $200 million cash cushion); the Abernathy JV had approximately $1.5 billion of gross cash with $268 million of CapEx complete and $1.1 billion remaining, backed by a $1.35 billion lump sum EPC contract. Both projects are fully funded through substantial completion and management does not anticipate needing additional equity for currently contracted development.
quarterly_data.figure: over $12.8 billion HPC leases signed and $6.5 billion financing in 2H25; $3.7 billion cash and restricted cash; WULF Compute $850 million CapEx complete / $2.38 billion remaining; Abernathy $268 million complete / $1.1 billion remaining; $1.35 billion lump sum EPC

quarterly_data.signal: Kentucky (Hawesville) point-in-time status before any lease was signed (CEO Paul Prager / CTO Khan / CFO Fleury): demand is extremely strong - every major hyperscaler and several large AI compute platforms are doing diligence in an open data room, with some written term sheets received; Prager expected a world-class credit as the next customer on what TeraWulf hopes will be a 10- to 15-year deal, 'pretty soon'. TeraWulf is targeting 1, maybe 2 customers for the 480-megawatt campus, and CFO Fleury said it is targeting 480 megawatts online in the second half of 2027; Fluor was brought on as EPC and has received a limited notice to proceed. Since year-end TeraWulf added approximately 1.5 gigawatts of power-backed capacity in Kentucky and Maryland; separately, in 2025 it secured up to 400 megawatts at the retired Cayuga coal facility (zoning approved; planning-board application being finalized).
quarterly_data.figure: 480 megawatts targeted online in the second half of 2027; 10- to 15-year deal targeted; approximately 1.5 gigawatts added in Kentucky and Maryland; Cayuga up to 400 megawatts

quarterly_data.signal: Morgantown / Chesapeake Data (Maryland) plan (CEO Prager / CTO Khan): Phase 1 includes approximately 500 megawatts of new dispatchable generation, 250 megawatts of battery storage and 500 megawatts of data center load, followed by a similar Phase 2, engineered to be a net generator to the state (about 0.5 megawatt of storage per megawatt of load). Cost build-up: data center $8 million to $10 million per megawatt (same range as Lake Mariner, Abernathy and Kentucky), gas-fired generation $2 million to $3 million per megawatt and roughly another $1 million per megawatt for batteries - all in around $13 million to $14 million per megawatt, to be charged back to the tenant in the capacity payment. FERC approval expected within 3 to 6 months; timing positioned as end of '28 / '29 and beyond, pending remediation scoping. Prager: 'The AI build-out is not constrained by GPUs. It is constrained by power, interconnection, transmission and increasingly new generation.'
quarterly_data.figure: Phase 1: approximately 500 megawatts generation, 250 megawatts of battery storage, 500 megawatts of data center load; all-in $13 million to $14 million per megawatt; FERC approval within 3 to 6 months

quarterly_data.signal: Growth guidance (CTO Khan / CEO Prager): TeraWulf targets 250 to 500 megawatts of incremental contracted critical IT capacity per year, which Khan equated to $2.5 billion to $5 billion of incremental capital per year for the next few years, delivered 12 to 18 months after signing; about 1.5 years earlier the guidance was 100 to 150. Management says it already controls the sites needed to deliver that range through the end of the decade. Standard building block: roughly 200-megawatt gross / 160-megawatt net critical IT per building (the Fluidstack base design is 168 megawatts of critical IT).
quarterly_data.figure: 250 to 500 megawatts per year; $2.5 billion to $5 billion of incremental capital per year; prior guidance 100 to 150

quarterly_data.signal: Site efficiency (CTO Khan): TeraWulf's northern sites are designed to a 1.25 PUE, helped by ambient conditions and extra cooling design headroom, while Abernathy (Texas) is at 1.4 PUE. Brownfield industrial sites with multiple independent power lines (5 lines into the Hawesville former smelter site) remove the need for large on-site diesel backup generation.

connects_to.relationship: Lake Mariner (NY) HPC data-center lease tenant

contracts.signal: CEO Prager: TeraWulf signed a 450-megawatt lease with Fluidstack supported by Google's credit, a 'platform-defining deal'; with its warrants Google will be TeraWulf's largest shareholder.

CTO Khan / CFO Fleury: CB3 is expected to deliver in mid-May after tenant design optimizations that did not change footprint or lease economics; CB4 and CB5, co-designed with Fluidstack, target lease commencement in the third and fourth quarter of 2026. Design optimization raised critical IT from 162 megawatts to 168 megawatts per building without changing the base construction budget, expected to add approximately $200 million of lease revenue over the initial term, while schedule adjustments cut projected 2025-2026 revenue by approximately $16 million.
contracts.units: 162 megawatts to 168 megawatts per building (CB4, CB5)
contracts.value: approximately $200 million of additional lease revenue over the initial term
